summary: At Iconium they speak in the synagogue "that a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed," while unbelievers make the Gentiles' minds "evil affected against the brethren." They stay "long time" nonetheless, "speaking boldly in the Lord," who "granted signs and wonders to be done by their hands," until the city divides and an assault is prepared "to use them despitefully, and to stone them." Fleeing to Lystra and Derbe, they preach; Paul sees a cripple "from his mother’s womb," perceives "that he had faith to be healed," and says, "Stand upright on thy feet," and "he leaped and walked." The crowd cries "in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men," and the priest of Jupiter brings "oxen and garlands." The apostles "rent their clothes," run in and protest, "We also are men of like passions with you," urging them to "turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea," who "left not himself without witness" in "rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons." Barely restrained, the same crowd is soon turned by Jews from Antioch and Iconium, and Paul is stoned and dragged out "supposing he had been dead," yet rises and goes on. Returning through those cities they confirm the disciples, teaching that "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God," ordain "elders in every church," pray with fasting, and report at Antioch how God "had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles."
takeaways: The crowd that would sacrifice to Paul stones him soon after. Adulation and violence lie closer together than they appear, and the apostles refuse both by insisting they are "men of like passions with you."

Paul's appeal to rain, fruitful seasons, and hearts filled "with food and gladness" grants that God has always given the nations a real witness of himself, so the gospel arrives naming a Giver they have long been receiving from.

The apostles do not promise exemption from suffering; they interpret it. Tribulation is the road into the kingdom rather than evidence of having wandered off it, which is why the same word that converts also confirms.

Evangelization does not end at conversion. They walk back through hostile cities to strengthen believers and appoint elders, so that new churches receive both continuing care and a settled ordering before the founders leave.

crossRefs.label: Acts 3:1-10 — Peter heals a man lame from his mother's womb, who goes walking and leaping
crossRefs.why: Luke tells an almost identical healing through Peter, down to the lifelong lameness and the leaping. The deliberate parallel presents Paul's ministry among the Gentiles as continuous in power and pattern with Peter's among the Jews.

crossRefs.label: Acts 17:22-31 — Paul at Athens preaches the God who made the world and gives all things
crossRefs.why: Facing another pagan audience, Paul again starts from the Creator who gives "life, and breath, and all things" rather than from Israel's scriptures. Read together, the two speeches show a consistent method for addressing those with no biblical background.

crossRefs.label: Romans 1:19-23 — what may be known of God is manifest, yet the glory of God is exchanged for images
crossRefs.why: Paul argues that God's power is "clearly seen" in what he has made, and that idolatry is a turning of that knowledge into images. Lystra dramatizes the letter's claim, as a genuine act of God is immediately misread into a pagan story.

crossRefs.label: 2 Timothy 3:10-12 — persecutions which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra
crossRefs.why: Paul names these exact cities when reminding Timothy what he endured and that the Lord delivered him out of all of it. It confirms Luke's account from Paul's own memory and generalizes it: all who will live godly shall suffer persecution.

crossRefs.label: Titus 1:5 — ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee
crossRefs.why: Paul instructs a delegate to complete what is lacking by appointing elders city by city. The near-identical phrasing shows the practice of Acts 14 hardening into a standing instruction for how new churches are to be finished and governed.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the apostles ordaining "elders in every church," with prayer and fasting, is read as evidence that the apostolic mission deliberately provided a permanent ordered ministry able to continue after the founders departed, which grounds the Catholic understanding of apostolic succession and the ordination of presbyters for each local community.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that the apostles installed local leaders, but read the appointment as recognizing qualified men to teach and govern particular congregations rather than as transmitting a priestly order, and many stress that the elders are commended "to the Lord, on whom they believed" rather than to a chain of office. Both traditions agree that Christ's churches are not left leaderless and that such leadership is conferred through the Church rather than seized.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Paul's argument that God "left not himself without witness" in rain and fruitful seasons as support for the conviction that something true about God can be known by reason from the world he has made, so that grace comes to a nature already capable of receiving it rather than to a blank.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally acknowledge the same witness in creation but emphasize how little it accomplishes on its own, since it leaves people without excuse rather than leading them to God, and Lystra proves the point when a real miracle produces immediate idolatry. Both traditions affirm that creation truly testifies to its Maker and that the gospel must still be preached for anyone to know him rightly.
